qualification: NSSCO Economics 6145 (syllabus vNIED 2018; implementation 2019; first examination 2020, examined 2026)

items.prompt: Identify the relationship concerning buyers and the relationship concerning producers in a bread market.
items.canonical_answer: Demand concerns buyers; supply concerns producers.
marking_guidance: Characteristic (1): demand—buyers. Distinction (1): supply—producers.
objective_titles: Define and illustrate demand and supply

items.prompt: Define demand.
items.canonical_answer: The quantities consumers are willing and able to buy at different prices over a specified period, other things equal.
marking_guidance: Meaning/definition and essential element (1): The quantities consumers are willing and able to buy at different prices over a specified period, other things equal.
objective_titles: Describe demand

items.prompt: Identify the two purchasing conditions needed for an intention to count as demand.
items.canonical_answer: Willingness to buy and ability to pay.
marking_guidance: Feature (1): willingness. Distinction/second essential element (1): ability to pay.
objective_titles: Describe demand

items.prompt: Define supply.
items.canonical_answer: The quantities producers are willing and able to offer at different prices over a specified period, other things equal.
marking_guidance: Meaning/definition and essential element (1): The quantities producers are willing and able to offer at different prices over a specified period, other things equal.
objective_titles: Describe supply

items.prompt: Identify the two producer conditions needed for output to count as supply.
items.canonical_answer: Willingness to offer it and ability to supply it under the stated conditions.
marking_guidance: Feature (1): willingness to offer. Distinction/second essential element (1): ability to supply.
objective_titles: Describe supply

items.prompt: Invented weekly market for bread rolls at the fictional Erongo Oven Stall in Namibia. Prices in N$ per roll: 4, 6, 8, 10, 12. Quantities demanded in rolls per week: 120, 100, 80, 60, 40. Quantities supplied: 40, 60, 80, 100, 120, respectively. Explain equilibrium using a diagram constructed from these schedules. Include the quantity imbalance at N$6 and the direction of price pressure if competitive adjustment is possible.
items.canonical_answer: Plot price vertically and quantity horizontally; label D and S. The original equilibrium is N$8 and 80 rolls. At N$6, Qd is 100 and Qs is 60, so excess demand is 40. The shortage can put upward pressure on price towards equilibrium.
marking_guidance: Axes/labels (1): N$ per roll and rolls per week. Original curves (2): correct D (1), correct S (1). Original equilibrium (1): N$8/80. Change/control (1): compare at N$6, not a curve shift. Explanation/interpretation (2): excess demand of 40 (1), upward price pressure under competitive adjustment (1). Total 7.
objective_titles: Discuss and illustrate the principle of equilibrium price

items.prompt: Invented weekly market for bread rolls at the fictional Erongo Oven Stall in Namibia. Prices in N$ per roll: 4, 6, 8, 10, 12. Quantities demanded in rolls per week: 120, 100, 80, 60, 40. Quantities supplied: 40, 60, 80, 100, 120, respectively. Analyse the imbalance at N$10 and the possible adjustment towards equilibrium.
items.canonical_answer: At N$10 supply is 100 rolls and demand 60, so excess supply is 40. Unsold offers can encourage sellers to reduce price; a lower price raises quantity demanded and reduces quantity supplied along the existing curves towards their intersection.
marking_guidance: Relationship/pattern (1): excess supply. Evidence/comparison (1): 100 offered versus 60 demanded, gap 40. Explanation/reason (2): unsold offers create downward pressure (1), movements along existing curves can close the gap (1). Total 4.
objective_titles: Discuss and illustrate the principle of equilibrium price

items.prompt: Invented weekly market for bread rolls at the fictional Erongo Oven Stall in Namibia. Prices in N$ per roll: 4, 6, 8, 10, 12. Quantities demanded in rolls per week: 120, 100, 80, 60, 40. Quantities supplied: 40, 60, 80, 100, 120, respectively. New quantities demanded at the same prices: 160, 140, 120, 100, 80. Supply is unchanged. Explain the change using a diagram of the original and new equilibria.
items.canonical_answer: Plot D and S from original data, then D1 to the right using the new demand schedule. D/S meet at N$8/80; D1/S meet at N$10/100. The demand increase creates excess demand at the original price, so the new equilibrium moves along unchanged supply to a higher price and quantity.
marking_guidance: Axes/labels (1): correct units. Original curves (2): correct D (1), S (1). Original equilibrium (1): N$8/80. Change (1): D1 right with S fixed. New equilibrium (1): N$10/100. Explanation/interpretation (1): increased demand raises price/quantity through movement along supply. Total 7.
objective_titles: Analyse simple market situations with changes in supply and demand

items.prompt: Invented weekly market for bread rolls at the fictional Erongo Oven Stall in Namibia. Prices in N$ per roll: 4, 6, 8, 10, 12. Quantities demanded in rolls per week: 120, 100, 80, 60, 40. Quantities supplied: 40, 60, 80, 100, 120, respectively. New quantities supplied at the same prices: 80, 100, 120, 140, 160. Demand is unchanged. Analyse the equilibrium change and distinguish the changed relationship from movement along a curve.
items.canonical_answer: Supply increases at each price, shifting S right. The original equilibrium N$8/80 becomes N$6/100. The fall in price increases quantity demanded along unchanged D; demand has not shifted.
marking_guidance: Relationship/pattern (1): supply shifts right. Evidence/comparison (1): N$8/80 to N$6/100. Explanation/reason (2): production conditions offer more at each price (1), lower price produces movement along unchanged demand (1). Total 4.
objective_titles: Analyse simple market situations with changes in supply and demand

items.prompt: Invented weekly market for bread rolls at the fictional Erongo Oven Stall in Namibia. Prices in N$ per roll: 4, 6, 8, 10, 12. Quantities demanded in rolls per week: 120, 100, 80, 60, 40. Quantities supplied: 40, 60, 80, 100, 120, respectively. Explain the error in shifting demand left merely to show an imposed maximum price of N$6. No demand or supply determinant changes.
items.canonical_answer: The control selects a price on the existing curves; it does not alter the underlying schedules. At N$6 demand is 100 and supply 60, so the control creates a shortage of 40 rather than a demand shift.
marking_guidance: Confusion/boundary (1): imposed price differs from determinant/curve shift. Test to distinguish (1): compare quantities on unchanged schedules at the controlled price.
objective_titles: Analyse simple market situations with changes in supply and demand

items.prompt: Identify one non-price determinant of bread demand and one determinant of bread supply.
items.canonical_answer: Buyers’ income for demand; flour input cost for supply.
marking_guidance: Feature/example (1): buyers’ income. Distinction (1): flour cost is a producer/supply condition.
objective_titles: Discuss the causes of changes in demand and supply conditions

items.prompt: Explain the distinction between a rise in buyers’ income and a rise in flour costs as causes of changes in the bread market. Assume bread is a normal good.
items.canonical_answer: Higher income can increase buyers’ demand at each price; higher flour costs can reduce producers’ supply at each price. One changes buyers’ conditions and the other production costs.
marking_guidance: Confusion/difference (1): buyer condition versus producer condition. Test to distinguish (1): identify which side offers/buys a different quantity at the same price.
objective_titles: Discuss the causes of changes in demand and supply conditions

items.prompt: Explain the difference between an income rise shifting demand for a normal good and the availability of substitutes affecting its price responsiveness.
items.canonical_answer: The income rise changes quantity demanded at each price and shifts demand. Substitute availability helps explain how strongly quantity demanded responds to the good’s own price; it is not the same question as a specified income-driven shift.
marking_guidance: Confusion/boundary (1): position/demand shift versus responsiveness. Test to distinguish (1): compare non-price change at each price with response to an own-price change.
objective_titles: Discuss the causes of changes in demand and supply conditions

items.prompt: Explain how higher income can increase demand for bread rolls when they are a normal good and other demand conditions are unchanged.
items.canonical_answer: Higher income gives buyers more purchasing power. For the stated normal good, they are willing and able to buy more at each price, shifting demand right and potentially raising equilibrium price and quantity if supply is unchanged and upward sloping.
marking_guidance: Starting change (1): higher income. Because/mechanism (1): greater purchasing power for a normal good. Relationship (1): more demanded at each price/right shift. Consequence (1): higher equilibrium price/quantity with stated supply conditions. Total 4.
objective_titles: Explain changes in demand conditions through a developed economic reason and consequence.

items.prompt: Explain the demand change for bread if a stated substitute becomes more expensive, with bread’s own price and other conditions unchanged.
items.canonical_answer: Some buyers switch towards bread, so more bread is demanded at each price and its demand curve shifts right.
marking_guidance: Context (1): substitute dearer at unchanged bread price. Reason/conclusion (1): switching increases bread demand at each price.
objective_titles: Explain changes in demand conditions through a developed economic reason and consequence.

items.prompt: Explain how cheaper flour can increase bread supply, other production and demand conditions unchanged.
items.canonical_answer: Lower input cost reduces the cost of making bread. More output can be worthwhile at the same selling prices, shifting supply right. With downward-sloping demand unchanged, the new equilibrium has a lower price and greater quantity.
marking_guidance: Starting change (1): cheaper flour. Because/mechanism (1): lower production cost. Relationship (1): more supplied at each price/right shift. Consequence (1): lower equilibrium price and higher quantity with stated demand. Total 4.
objective_titles: Explain changes in supply conditions through a developed economic reason and consequence.

items.prompt: Explain the supply effect of an increase in flour cost for an invented bread seller, with the bread price and other conditions unchanged.
items.canonical_answer: The higher input cost makes production less attractive at that price, so less is offered at each price and supply contracts left.
marking_guidance: Context (1): flour cost rises. Reason/conclusion (1): lower quantity offered at each price contracts supply.
objective_titles: Explain changes in supply conditions through a developed economic reason and consequence.

items.prompt: Invented weekly market for bread rolls at the fictional Erongo Oven Stall in Namibia. Prices in N$ per roll: 4, 6, 8, 10, 12. Quantities demanded in rolls per week: 120, 100, 80, 60, 40. Quantities supplied: 40, 60, 80, 100, 120, respectively. New quantities supplied after an input-cost increase at the same prices: 0, 20, 40, 60, 80. Demand is unchanged. Explain the price and quantity change using a constructed diagram.
items.canonical_answer: Plot original D/S at N$8/80. Plot S2 left using the new supply schedule. Its intersection with D is N$10/60. Higher production cost contracts supply, raising the equilibrium price but reducing the quantity traded along unchanged demand.
marking_guidance: Axes/labels (1): N$ per roll and rolls per week. Original curves (2): correct D (1), S (1). Original equilibrium (1): N$8/80. Change (1): S2 left due to input cost. New equilibrium (1): N$10/60. Explanation/interpretation (1): price rises and quantity falls with D unchanged. Total 7.
objective_titles: Analyse such changes to show effects on price

items.prompt: Invented weekly market for bread rolls at the fictional Erongo Oven Stall in Namibia. Prices in N$ per roll: 4, 6, 8, 10, 12. Quantities demanded in rolls per week: 120, 100, 80, 60, 40. Quantities supplied: 40, 60, 80, 100, 120, respectively. New quantities supplied after an input-cost increase at the same prices: 0, 20, 40, 60, 80. Demand is unchanged. Analyse the implications of the equilibrium change for buyers and sellers. Do not infer profit from price alone.
items.canonical_answer: Equilibrium changes from N$8/80 to N$10/60. Buyers face a higher price and fewer rolls. Sellers receive a higher price per roll but trade fewer, while input costs have risen, so a higher price alone cannot establish a gain in receipts or profit.
marking_guidance: Relationship/pattern (1): higher price, lower traded quantity. Evidence/comparison (1): N$8/80 versus N$10/60. Explanation/reason (2): buyers’ affordability/availability worsens (1), seller gains cannot be inferred without quantity/cost effects (1). Total 4.
objective_titles: Analyse such changes to show effects on price

items.prompt: Define demand (2). Invented weekly market for bread rolls at the fictional Erongo Oven Stall in Namibia. Prices in N$ per roll: 4, 6, 8, 10, 12. Quantities demanded in rolls per week: 120, 100, 80, 60, 40. Quantities supplied: 40, 60, 80, 100, 120, respectively. Identify the equilibrium price and quantity (2). Explain one non-price cause of increased demand for bread rolls, stating any needed normal-good condition (2). Identify two supply determinants (2).
items.canonical_answer: Demand combines willingness and ability to buy at alternative prices over a period, other things equal. Equilibrium is N$8 and 80 rolls. Higher income can increase demand if bread is a normal good, with other conditions unchanged. Flour costs and suitable technology are supply determinants.
marking_guidance: Meaning (2): willingness/ability (1), quantities at prices over a period/other things equal (1). Separate points for equilibrium (2): N$8 (1), 80 rolls (1). Explanation (2): higher income/purchasing power (1), increased demand for normal bread under stated conditions (1). Supply determinants (2): input costs (1), technology (1). Marks allocation 8.

items.prompt: Invented weekly market for bread rolls at the fictional Erongo Oven Stall in Namibia. Prices in N$ per roll: 4, 6, 8, 10, 12. Quantities demanded in rolls per week: 120, 100, 80, 60, 40. Quantities supplied: 40, 60, 80, 100, 120, respectively. New quantities demanded at the same prices: 160, 140, 120, 100, 80. Supply is unchanged. Describe three features of the original demand/supply schedules (6). Explain the new equilibrium and the adjustment from the original price (7). Discuss effects on buyers and sellers, contrasting the demand increase with a supply contraction caused by higher input costs. For the contraction, supplied quantities are 0, 20, 40, 60 and 80 at the stated prices and original demand applies (7).
items.canonical_answer: The original schedule specifies willingness/ability at alternative prices and a common weekly product quantity; demand slopes down and supply up. Increased demand shifts D right; at N$8 the new demand of 120 exceeds supply of 80, creating upward pressure. The new equilibrium is N$10 and 100 rolls. A supply contraction instead meets original demand at N$10 and 60. Both raise price but quantity differs. Demand growth can expand selling opportunities while buyers face a higher price; cost-driven contraction reduces availability and burdens producers with higher costs. Judge gains by the cause, affected agent and costs rather than the price sign alone.
marking_guidance: Context/data description (6): alternative prices (1), N$ per roll stated (1); common quantities/period (1), rolls per week (1); demand falls as own price rises (1), supply rises along original schedule (1). Mechanism/explanation (7): D shifts right (1), at N$8 new Qd120 (1), Qs80 (1), excess demand40 (1), upward price pressure (1), new price N$10 (1), quantity100 (1). Both sides/judgement (7): demand case price/quantity both higher (1), supply case price higher but quantity60 (1); buyers face higher price (1), demand growth expands seller opportunities (1); contraction brings higher costs/lower availability (1); no universal winner from price alone (1), conclude using agent/cause/cost conditions (1). Marks allocation 6+7+7=20.

items.prompt: Evaluate the consequences of two changes in an invented bread market in separate seven-mark plans. Original equilibrium is N$8 and 80 rolls per week. Case 1: preferences shift demand right with supply unchanged, producing N$10 and 100 rolls. Case 2: higher flour cost contracts supply with demand unchanged, producing N$10 and 60 rolls. Consider buyers, sellers, the cause of the change and the limits of judging benefit from price alone.
items.canonical_answer: Case 1: more wanted output can be traded, benefiting sellers’ opportunities and buyers who obtain additional output. Existing buyers face a higher price. Judge seller benefit subject to costs and the ability to supply, while recognising the distributional effect on buyers. Case 2: sellers receive more per roll but sell fewer and face higher input costs; buyers face less availability and a higher price. This is less favourable for buyers and cannot be assumed beneficial to producers. The decisive conditions are quantity response and costs, rather than the shared price increase.
marking_guidance: Case 1 allocation (7): argument for more wanted output traded (1), expanded seller opportunity (1); argument against higher buyer price (1), producers still need capacity/resources (1); condition costs/capacity relative to demand gain (1); judgement conditional seller gain (1), acknowledge buyer affordability trade-off (1). Case 2 marks (7): argument for higher receipts per roll (1), possible partial recovery of cost pressure (1); argument against fewer rolls traded (1), higher input costs and buyer price burden (1); condition quantity and cost effects (1); judgement rejects automatic seller gain (1), identifies adverse buyer availability/affordability (1). Total 14.
objective_titles: Discuss and illustrate the principle of equilibrium price
Discuss the causes of changes in demand and supply conditions
